question: What is the meaning of energy performance certificate (epc) in relation to official (mandated) indicators and certificates?
description: An energy performance certificate (EPC) is a document that shows the energy efficiency rating of a building or property. It provides information on the energy performance of the building, typically using a standardized scale or rating system. EPCs are often based on official (mandated) indicators and certificates, such as those required by regulations or standards set by governing bodies. These indicators and certificates help assess and communicate the energy efficiency of a building to potential buyers, tenants, or other stakeholders.

The internationally recognized and accepted classification system for 
labels is issued by the ISO 14020 standard and categorizes labels into 
three types based on their verification (ISO, 2021b), self declarations 
(ISO, 2021a), and LCA data (ISO, 2021c). Eco-certificates and 
eco-labels frequently coincide, hence, the terms are often ’incor­
rectly’ used interchangeably to refer to the combination of concepts 
while concepts technically can exist independently. 
The key difference between certificates is that (1) an eco-certificate 
displays the environmental performance of a product on a static 
collected life cycle inventory while passport is a dynamic registration 
that takes place during the life cycle of a product, (2) not necessarily, but 
typically an eco-certificate is assigned to a product design, rather than a 
unique object, and (3) a passport attempts to valuate a product. 
3.6. Contents 
Passports appear in variants, for instance, with a focus on specific 
type of objects (e.g., buildings (Debacker and Manshoven, 2016), in­
frastructures (Wittenveen & Bos, 2018), clothing (Riedelsheimer et al., 
2020)) or with a specific purpose (e.g., renovation (Sesana et al., 2021), 
recycling (Spengler and Schr¨oter, 2003), optimizing operational use (Ye 
et al., 2020)). Passport requirements typically shape along with the 
intended product application. For example, a passport of a large com­
mercial company structure may not need the same level of detail as one 
for small residential buildings (Gonçalves et al., 2021; Transitieteam 
CBE, 2020; Wittenveen & Bos, 2018). Fig. 5 provides an overview of the 
attributes (lower level) that passports can typically consist of. This sup­
ports in deriving more holistic understanding of the typical components 
(higher-level) of a concept (bold text in Fig. 5 or see Fig. A4 and Table A6 
in Appendix A4). 
Nearly every passport contains a digital representation of the phys­
ical composition and technical characteristics of an object (C.12). 
Frequently reported data attributes are: information regarding the 
quality conditions of an object (C.1), the servicing history of an object 
(C.20), guidelines for maintenance, safety and recycling (C.13-C.18) and 
the valuation of an object (C.3). Performance indicators are also 
commonly part of a passport, but not all passports offer such metrics to 
measure the environmental performance of the object. EPDs and energy 
certificates are most frequently observed. Remarkable is the usual lack 
of circularity indicators (Moraga et al., 2019) reported while these align 
well with one of the key passport goals. A possible explanation is that 
sustainability and circularity indicators may introduce subjectivity both 
by focusing on specific aspects of sustainability or circularity and can 
apply weight to the objective results in selected indicator formula’s 
(Moraga et al., 2019). Moreover, for the sole purpose of identifying the 
value for use, recovery, and reuse, indicators may be helpful, but not 
always strictly required. There are two popular decision support attri­
butes in passports. Firstly, tools to explore options for recovery and 
renovation (C.49) which support object governance by letting users’ 
compare known alternative treatments. Secondly, scenario modelling 
(C.50) allows users to reason about unknown future states of the object 
which may help to identify a CE governance strategy. 
3.7. Stakeholders 
Since passports are about the governance of the entire product life 
cycle, it may be helpful to understand who the involved actors are, what 
their role is and perspective they hold toward passports. We choose to 
anchor the actor analysis to the most frequently used life cycle variant 
(Stark, 2015, p. 7).

Article 19
Other markings and performance claims
1.
Markings other than the CE marking, including private ones, may be affixed to a product only if they do not indicate 
that the product’s performance in relation to essential characteristics covered by applicable harmonised technical 
specifications had to be assessed in a way different from that laid down by this Regulation.
Officially recognised EN ISO 14024 type I ecolabels may be affixed to a product if they fulfil the requirement in the first 
subparagraph.
2.
Markings allowed in accordance with paragraph 1 and other markings set out by Union legislation may be affixed to 
a product provided that they do not impair the visibility, legibility and meaning of the CE marking.
3.
Where a product is covered by a harmonised technical specification, a claim made by an economic operator about the 
product’s performance, which concerns an essential characteristic covered by that harmonised technical specification, shall 
comply with the assessment method for that particular essential characteristic as laid down in the harmonised technical 
specifications.
4.
Where a product is covered by harmonised technical specifications, claims about its performance in relation to the 
essential characteristics laid down in those harmonised technical specifications may be additionally provided in a place 
other than in the declaration of performance and conformity only if they are already provided in the declaration of 
performance and conformity.
The first subparagraph shall not apply to situations where, in accordance with Article 14, no declaration of performance 
and conformity has been drawn up.
CHAPTER III
OBLIGATIONS AND RIGHTS OF ECONOMIC OPERATORS
Article 20
Obligations of all economic operators
1.
The obligations of economic operators under this Chapter are applicable only in relation to products covered by 
a harmonised technical specification, or to products that have been CE-marked on the basis of a European technical 
assessment.
2.
An economic operator shall take all necessary measures to ensure continued compliance with this Regulation. Where 
non-compliance of the economic operator or of a product has been stated and corrective action has been requested by 
a market surveillance authority in accordance with Article 65(1), the economic operator shall submit progress reports to 
that authority until that authority decides that the corrective action can be closed.
3.
An economic operator shall, on request of a competent national authority, identify to that authority any economic 
operator or other actor:
(a) who has supplied that economic operator with a product, including components or spare parts of products, and the 
quantity of that supply, or who has supplied it with a service covered by this Regulation;
(b) to whom that economic operator has supplied a product, including components or spare parts of products, and the 
quantity of that supply, or to whom it has supplied a service covered by this Regulation.
When identifying the economic operators or other actors referred to in the first subparagraph, an economic operator shall 
inform the competent national authority of, at least, the following:
(a) the contact details, including addresses and email addresses of those economic operators or actors;
(b) the tax and company registration numbers of those economic operators or actors.
4.
